drapeaux.note: « ressusciter et démystifier le catastrophisme légendaire » : citation donnée en français, retraduite vers l'anglais ; langue d'origine probable anglais, auteur J Harlen Bretz (discours de la médaille Penrose, 1979).

titre: Bretz and the Washington State flood: a debate over method
accroche: In 1923, Bretz attributes the Channeled Scablands to a flood. His peers were rejecting a principle, not the facts.
contenu_vulgarise:
The story is famous: a lone geologist proposes a gigantic flood, his peers mock him, and he ends up being right. It is less simple, and more instructive.

## A landscape that can't be explained

J Harlen Bretz (no period after the J) was born in 1882 in Michigan. A high school teacher in Seattle from 1907, he earned a doctorate at Chicago in 1913, then taught field geology. During the summers of 1922 and 1923, with his students, he described in eastern Washington State a set of strange forms: coulees, dry cataracts, rock basins, anastomosing channels, gravel bars. Multilevel divide crossings lead him to an idea: a cataclysmic flood swept across the Columbia Plateau at the end of the Pleistocene. He calls it the “Spokane Flood,” and concludes in 1923: “It was a debacle which swept the Columbia Plateau.”

## A problem of method, not first of evidence

The disagreement is not only about facts. The geologists of the day hold the principle of uniformity as the foundation of their science: cataclysmic phenomena are not proper objects of study. Bretz knows it. He answers with fieldwork: more than a dozen major papers between 1923 and 1932. And he gets published, because he has just been granted tenure and, right before submitting his paper, joined the editorial board of the *Journal of Geology*.

## A water source was missing

After a decade of fieldwork, Bretz leaves the subject in 1933 and counts on others to settle it. What follows comes from Joseph Pardee, who documents glacial Lake Missoula, held back by an ice dam, as a plausible source. According to the history of Washington State from HistoryLink, this lake would have held some 530 cubic miles of water behind a wall of ice more than 2,000 feet high, and the floods would have numbered about a hundred during the last glaciation, roughly 20,000 to 13,000 years ago.

The evidence accumulates, and according to Baker, the immense gravel current ripples capping buttes that Bretz had described as river bars weigh heavily with skeptics. By the late 1960s and early 1970s, the hypothesis is generally accepted.

## What he takes from it

In 1979, at age 97, Bretz receives the Penrose Medal of the Geological Society of America. In his remarks he sums up his contribution: having helped to “resurrect and demystify legendary catastrophism” and having challenged an overly rigid uniformitarianism. What changes the skeptics' minds is not a conversion: it is a plausible cause, then fieldwork.

repere.texte: J Harlen Bretz proposes a “Spokane Flood” in 1923 to explain the Channeled Scablands, and publishes more than a dozen major papers between 1923 and 1932. The hypothesis is generally accepted in the late 1960s and early 1970s; he receives the Penrose Medal in 1979, at age 97.
repere.source: Victor R. Baker, “J Harlen Bretz (1882–1981),” GSA Today, May 2022

carte.punch: Bretz was not censored: his peers were rejecting a principle, not first the facts.
carte.idee: In 1923, J Harlen Bretz attributes the Channeled Scablands to a cataclysmic flood. His paper is published, but it clashes with the dominant uniformitarianism. Lake Missoula, held back by an ice dam, later provides the plausible source.

quiz.question: According to Baker, what mainly led to the acceptance of Bretz's hypothesis?
choix: A change in the Geological Society's definition of uniformitarianism
A vote of geologists after Bretz's death, in 1981
Records from an eyewitness of the great flood described in 1923
A plausible water source, Lake Missoula, then field evidence such as the current ripples
quiz.explication: Pardee documents glacial Lake Missoula, held back by an ice dam, as a plausible source. The gravel current ripples capping buttes described by Bretz are among the evidence that convinces the skeptics.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why was Bretz's paper able to appear in 1923 despite its boldness?
choix: He had published it at his own expense, outside any scholarly journal
He had just been granted tenure and joined the editorial board of the journal that published him
The journal did not read papers by its own professors
No reviewer was interested, the region being judged unimportant
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Baker notes two assets: Bretz had been granted tenure shortly before formulating it, and just before submitting his paper to the Journal of Geology, he had joined its editorial board.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did the principle of uniformity call into question in Bretz's work?
choix: The date of the Earth's formation, judged too old
The very existence of the Pleistocene glaciations
The idea that a cataclysmic event could explain an entire landscape
The possibility of doing field geology without theory
quiz_supplementaire.explication: For the geologists of the day, cataclysmic phenomena were not good subjects of study: the principle of uniformity was held to be the foundation of their science. Bretz knew it, and answered with years of fieldwork.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Bretz do after his decade of work on the Scablands?
choix: He moves away from it in 1933 to other subjects, counting on others to settle it
He gives up geology for secondary-school teaching
He continues alone in the field until his death in 1981
He disowns his hypothesis after his peers' criticism
quiz_supplementaire.explication: He leaves the debate to others, convinced that other field studies would resolve it, and devotes himself to Greenland's glaciers and then, from 1938 to 1961, to the origin of limestone caves.
